qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: A produce vendor sorted the morning delivery into separate bins — apples in one, oranges in another, pears in a third — so shoppers could find each fruit quickly. No bin was treated as higher, better, or lower than any other; they simply sat side by side on the stand. Is 'stratification' the precise word for how the vendor arranged the fruit?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Yes — 'stratification' fits, because the fruit was separated into clearly distinct groups.
Yes — 'stratification' fits, because there are three categories, and three is enough to form layers.
No — the bins sit side by side as equals; stratification would set them in tiers, one over the next, like the cabin classes on an airline.
No — 'hierarchy' is the precise word, because the vendor personally decided where each bin would go.

qti-content-body.p: Right. The bins are equal groups set side by side — no bin outranks any other. Stratification requires tiers ordered from top to bottom, like an airline's first, business, and economy cabins; the fruit stand has nothing of the kind, so the word doesn't fit.

Stratification requires more than separate groups — it requires tiers ordered above and below one another, like an airline's cabin classes. The vendor's bins are equals, none outranking the rest, so 'stratification' doesn't fit; and 'hierarchy' fails for the same reason, since choosing where bins physically sit creates no ranking among them.
